title: Play C then A minor on a ukulele: four even downstrokes on each chord, every string ringing at the right pitch
instruction: Play the ukulele: strum four even downstrokes on a C chord (A string held at the third fret), then change to A minor (G string held at the second fret) and strum four more on the same beat.
context: The ukulele is a mass-market first instrument: more than 1.7 million were sold in the US in 2021 (Statista, from The Music Trades; link in the README), and it is taught in school music classes. Beginner methods start with exactly these chords: Kjos's 'Ukulele for All' class method gives its first chord chapters to C and A minor (then F), with strumming exercises on each. It is more than a key press: one hand must press a single string just behind the fret wire, hard enough to seat it on the crown (lighter or farther back and it buzzes) and without touching the next string 10 mm away; the other hand must sweep across all four strings in one stroke, catching each and letting it snap free so it rings, neither grazing it nor slapping it into the frets; the strokes must keep an even beat, and the fretting hand must move to the new chord (a different string, a different fret) between two beats without muting the strings still ringing.
setup: Positions in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. A soprano ukulele (all mahogany, 53 cm overall, 346 mm scale, 250 x 162 x 60 mm body, 50 mm soundhole) lies on its back in a padded instrument cradle (two 30 mm black foam pads under the body and a foam neck rest under the headstock), clamped so it can't move. Its neck runs along y, centred on x = 0.36, headstock to the robot's right: the nut is at y = -0.16, the 3rd fret at y = -0.105, the 12th fret (where the body begins) at y = +0.013, the bridge saddle at y = +0.186 and the tail at y = +0.263. The rosewood fingerboard (35 mm wide at the nut, 43 mm at its end) is 95 mm above the table, with 15 nickel-silver frets (2.0 mm wide, 1.0 mm tall crowns) ending 4.5 mm past the 15th fret (y = +0.045). Bone nut and saddle. Strings: fluorocarbon, standard GCEA tuning (re-entrant G), at pitch: G 0.66 mm (34 N), C 0.84 mm (31 N), E 0.74 mm (30 N), A 0.61 mm (36 N); 27 mm from G to A at the nut and 42 mm at the saddle, the G string farthest from the robot and the A string nearest; string height above the frets 0.5 mm at the 1st fret, 1.0 mm at the 3rd, 2.5 mm at the 12th. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The strings are watched after every physics step (240 Hz) from their own motion, in the ukulele's frame: the load on each point of a string is its equation of motion read backwards (tension x bend, damping, inertia), i.e. what touches it. Stopped at fret n: fret n's crown bears at least 0.5 N and no crown beyond it is touched (a crown touched more lightly is a buzz); the vibrating length and pitch follow: C chord: A string at the 3rd fret, 291 mm, C5 523 Hz; G, C, E open, 346 mm, G4 392 Hz, C4 262 Hz, E4 330 Hz. Am chord: G string at the 2nd fret, 308 mm, A4 440 Hz; C, E, A open (A4 440 Hz). A press on the wire or behind the wrong fret gives the wrong stop. A string sounds when: something pushes it (at least 0.3 N) to a swing of at least 1 mm with nothing else touching it (0.15 N more than 25 mm away; the last 31 mm before the saddle is not watched); it is let go (back under 30% of the peak within 50 ms); it swings through its line to at least 30% of the peak on the other side; and for 0.5 s it rings with nothing touching it (no finger, fret or fingerboard: at least 0.15 N anywhere, or 35 N/m of the peak swing if more; free ringing reads up to 23 N/m) and its stop unchanged, or until the next strum plucks it again (no sooner than 0.4 s; the push must become a new pluck, let go within 50 ms). Before the chord change, the fretted string may be let off its fret 0.2 s after it was let go. A strum: plucks let go within 0.25 s of the first, of at least two strings. Only the first eight strums count (no retries): 1-4 must be C, 5-8 Am. A strum counts only if its fretted note sounds at the right fret (A on the 3rd for C, G on the 2nd for Am); otherwise it earns nothing (open strings strummed in time score 0). Score = 0.6 x the share of the 32 strings sounding at the chord's pitch in counting strums + 0.2 x the share of the 8 strums that count and have all four sounding, let go in order G, C, E, A + 0.2 x the share of the 7 gaps between two counting strums' onsets within 10% of the mean gap, the mean between 0.6 and 1.0 s (100 to 60 bpm). 0 if a string is ever pulled more than 12 mm out of line. 1.0 (success) when everything is met. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: from an audio recording and video, each strum's four pitches start in order G, C, E, A within 0.25 s, none missing or buzzing, each still ringing 0.5 s later (a tuner app reads C5 or A4 from the fretted string); beat evenness from the strum onsets.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Check the tuning (G4 C4 E4 A4) with a clip-on tuner before each trial. On a real ukulele the result is heard and checked with a tuner app or a phone recording: a clean chord rings G4, C4, E4 and C5 (523 Hz from the A string) together; a muted string is missing, a buzz or a wrong A (A4 open, C#5 at the 4th fret) is audible; slow-motion video shows the strum's order and timing.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz. One fixed body with full-size colliders: fingerboard, 15 fret wires, nut, saddle, body. Each string: 26 capsule nodes on sprung prismatic joints; springs of tension/span plus a saddle-end force make the taut-string equations, so finger, frets and strum touch the real string. Simplified: strings far heavier than real (87 g, with joint inertia, for solver stability), so a pluck swings at about 13 Hz, not 262-523 Hz; no sound; tension constant; instrument clamped.
